http://www.parisguardian.com/news/279225.text: Australia's sanctions aren't stopping Israel's settler funding Independent Australia 07 Aug 2026, 03:30 GMT+10 Despite three rounds of sanctions, Israel's financial support for the settler movement Australia targeted has continued to grow, writesWayne Hawkins. IN JULY 2024, Foreign Affairs MinisterPenny Wongannouncedsanctionson the Israeli settler networkHilltop Youthand seven of its members, citing beatings, sexual assault and torture of Palestinians. It wasn't a one-off. Australia has kept going: a second round in June 2025targetingIsraeli Finance MinisterBezalel Smotrichand National Security MinisterItamar Ben-Gvir, athird roundon 2 June 2026 adding three more individuals and four more entities including, for the first time, illegal farming outposts and ajoint statementon 9 June 2026 with the UK, Canada, France and Norway promising coordinated action against the networks that finance and enable settler violence. On paper, that looks like escalation. In practice,Al Jazeera reportsthe Israeli Government is now funding the same sanctioned movement to the tune of close to $40 million, on top of military protection and other state assistance. Three rounds of Australian sanctions, and the funding for the group they targeted has grown faster than the sanctions have. Despite diplomatic lobbying from the Israeli embassy, Labor delegates rejected efforts to dilute the party's stance on Gaza while shelving calls for stronger action against Israel. Part of the answer is structural and it's worth being precise about it rather than assuming bad faith. Hilltop Youth was never a registered organisation with a bank account to freeze it's a label for a loose, decentralised movement. When the U.S. Treasury sanctioned it in 2024, even theTimes of Israelnoted it was unclear the designation could be enforced, since there's no formal entity behind the name. Israel's stipend program follows that same seam: funds are paid to individual youths through regional councils, not to anything called Hilltop Youth. The sanctions were built for a movement; the payments go to people. But that only explains part of the $40 million. The harder case isHavat Gilad, a settler organisation that is explicitly under Western sanctions. Israel's National Security Ministry, run by Ben-Gvir, gave it $1.3 million anyway. Times of Israel reported it remains unclear whether that grant exposes the Israeli Government itself to secondary sanctions from the six Western governments involved.Peace Nowhas separately noted this is the first time Israel's government has funded the outposts this openly, while the responsible minister's office maintains the funding was coordinated with the Defence Ministry and lawful. So this isn't simply a loophole. In at least one case, it's money going straight to a named, sanctioned entity, with Israeli reporting itself asking whether that should trigger consequences nobody has yet imposed. In June 2026, Israel'sSettlement and National Missions Ministry, run byOrit Strook, confirmed a$1.9 million stipend program50 shekels (AU$23.45) a day, food vouchers, mediators for roughly 650 young settlers in illegal West Bank outposts, framed as violence prevention. Even then it was reported as a slice of a larger 120-million-shekel (AU$41.3 million) program. That larger figure is now confirmed, and theUN recorded over 1,330 settler attacksin the West Bank in just the first half of this year a period one of the movement's own leaders has described as a golden era. This isn't a fringe movement the Israeli State is failing to contain. Its founding call came from a foreign minister in 1998.Zvi Sukkot, a former Hilltop Youth figure, now chairs a Knesset committee. Ben-Gvir, the Minister whose ministry funded a sanctioned NGO, was himself convicted in 2007 of supporting a terrorist organisation and inciting violence. The movement Australia sanctioned has been substantially absorbed into the government we continue to treat as a full diplomatic and trading partner. The Royal Commission into Antisemitism has sparked debate over free speech, protest rights and the place of Palestinian perspectives in public discourse. None of this means Australia has done nothing; it means what Australia has done isn't landing. This is a structural problem, not a failure of any one minister or announcement: three escalating rounds of sanctions and the funding for the sanctioned movement has escalated faster than the sanctions could reach it. A commentary inMichael West Mediain June put it plainly, asking just how coordinated and effective these sanctions efforts have actually been, given settler violence has continued largely unopposed. A government can hold two positions that are formally consistent and practically hollow at the same time: we sanction this movement and we maintain full, unchanged diplomatic and trade relations with the state now funding it at record levels, including at least one payment to a name on our own sanctions list and call that a coherent Israel policy. It isn't. I've written before about resource sovereignty and about who actually holds power accountable to its stated commitments, locally in Tasmania and structurally in how governments behave when the mechanics of a policy stop matching its stated intent. This is the same pattern: a policy escalated on paper while the facts on the ground move faster in the opposite direction. Australians deserve sanctions that mean something. If ours do, our government owes the public an answer on how a movement it has sanctioned three times over is now better funded by Israel than at any point since those sanctions began and whether a payment to an entity already on our sanctions list changes anything. I've written to my local independent MP,Andrew Wilkie, asking that exact question be put on the record. It's a fair one to ask of every member of Parliament. Wayne Hawkinsis a small business owner in Hobart, Tasmania, and an independent candidate for the federal seat of Clark at the 2028 Election. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9qr.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, A major police operation has been mounted in Aarau, near Zurich By Rorey Bosotti Published 30 August 2026, 07:27 BST Updated 39 minutes ago A manhunt is under way after a 22-year-old woman was killed and five others injured in a shooting at a rave in Switzerland. The woman died at the scene in Aarau, police said. Those injured were four men and a woman aged between 24 and 27, all of whom are in hospital with injuries "ranging from minor to severe". Organisers and performers confirmed the shooting happened at a techno rave being held at a horse racing track in the town, which is located some 46km (29 miles) west of Zurich. Police said the perpetrator's identity and possible motives were unknown, as were the "exact circumstances" of the incident. Local media reported that the force was alerted to the shooting around 02:30 local time (01:30 BST). A DJ who was due to perform until the scheduled end of the event at 02:00 said the incident occurred "straight after our set", in a post on social media. Another performer, DJ Tekibo, said he had lost a friend in the incident. He wrote on Instagram that he was "still trying to process what happened". Olivier Grein, whose firm Agency Events AG organised the event, said the company was "shaken" and would do all it could to support police. Organisers had expected up to 3,500 people to attend. Police asked witnesses to submit photographs and video from the scene. An area around the racing track, the town's swimming pool and sports field has been cordoned off, with the public urged to stay away. A large contingent of officers has also been deployed beyond Aarau "as a precaution", Aargau Cantonal Police said. An AFP journalist reported seeing armed officers deployed on the highway up to 30km (18 miles) from the site of the shooting. Aarau is located some 46km west of Zurich and is home to approximately 23,000 people. It is also less than 40km (25 miles) from the border with Germany. German media reported that police on the German side have been providing support to Swiss forces as the manhunt continues. Image source, EPA Image caption, Armed officers were deployed near the scene early on Sunday Images from Aarau early on Sunday showed a heavy police presence in the area, with an armoured vehicle seen blocking a road. Armed police and officers in riot gear could be seen patrolling the streets. In addition to police and fire officials, the regional disaster response unit (KKE) was deployed, according to broadcaster SRF. It also reported that a Swiss Army helicopter could be seen surveying the area in the early hours. Switzerland has one for the highest rates of gun ownership in Europe, although violent shootings are rare and tighter controls were introduced in recent years. https://www.dw.com/en/victims-of-nazi-wa.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5PI3r Prefer DW on Google The former Nazi regime forced thousands of Polish people to work in Germany under inhumane conditions during World War II Image: picture alliance Advertisement "We can no longer wait," declared Polish victims' organizations in a dramatic appeal to German civil society, published on November 5 on the website of the Foundation for Polish–German Reconciliation. "Around 50,000 survivors of Nazi persecution during the German occupation still live in Poland today. They include former concentration camp and prison inmates, people deported to Germany for forced labor and those subjected to other forms of Nazi repression ," wrote the signatories of the appeal. The open letter pointed out that many of the survivors are over 90 years old, struggling with illness and rising costs, and in need of help in their daily lives. "For many, any further delay in deciding to provide assistance means that help will come too late," said the appeal, which was distributed in German, Polish and English. Unresolved issues of reparations have strained relations between Germany and Poland for decades Image: AP/picture alliance While Germany has recognized its moral responsibility toward the remaining survivors of Nazi persecution, the signatories pointed out that a corresponding decision on possible reparations by the German federal government has yet to be made. "Today, we appeal primarily to German civil society to provide humanitarian support to survivors of Nazi persecution living in Poland," they wrote, addressing businesses, foundations, associations and private citizens. "Every donation matters." Reparations offered to date seen as insufficient The unresolved issue of war reparations has clouded German-Polish relations for decades. Following the 1989 democratic transition in Central and Eastern Europe and the reunification of Germany, the federal government provided 500 million deutschmarks to Holocaust victims in Poland. More than 1 million people received support through these funds. Former forced laborers also received payments from the EVZ Foundation, which works to preserve the memory of the victims of National Socialist persecution. However, given the scale of German crimes during World War II, the reparations provided to date have been considered as insufficient by large parts of Polish society. German occupation policy in Poland was characterized by systematic crimes against the Polish population. An estimated 6 million Polish citizens were killed during the war, including about 3 million Polish Jews . At 100, Auschwitz survivor recalls life during the Holocaust To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video As part of the "General Plan East," a large portion of the population was to be displaced, enslaved or murdered. As early as 1939, the "Intelligenzaktion" specifically targeted the Polish elites, including teachers, clergy, civil servants and intellectuals. In addition, approximately 2.5 million Poles were deported to the German Reich for forced labor and made to work there under inhumane conditions. When it came to power in 2015, Poland's right-wing conservative Law and Justice Party (PiS) made the issue of war reparations a central focus of Warsaw's policy toward Berlin. The PiS government estimated Poland's war losses at 6.2 trillion zloty (approx. €1.3 trillion/$1.58 trillion) and officially demanded this sum from Berlin in October 2022. Tusk rejects €200 million as insufficient The center-left government led by Donald Tusk has distanced itself from these demands since Tusk's election victory in December 2023. However, the government has also made no secret of the fact that Poland is expecting a "creative solution" from its German partner, according to Foreign Minister Radek Sikorski. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk (front) has made no secret of the fact that he's waiting for a 'creative solution' from Germany Image: Kacper Pempel/REUTERS Former German Chancellor Olaf Scholz had offered €200 million ($224 million) prior to his visit to Poland in the summer of 2024, an offer rejected by Tusk as insufficient. The talks held since then between Berlin and Warsaw have failed to produce a solution. In a final declaration following the German-Polish government consultations in December 2025, the German government promised to "analyze possibilities for additional support for Polish victims of Nazi aggression and the German occupation of Poland." "Currently, there is no decision regarding a humanitarian gesture and the draft budget reflects this status," Josef Hinterseher, deputy spokesperson for Germany's Federal Foreign Office, told reporters on September 23. Germany's Greens still hope for 'humanitarian gesture' Germany's opposition Greens party has not given up hope of a turnaround in its efforts to secure a "humanitarian gesture." "Our parliamentary group submitted a request to the budget committee to secure funding for this 'humanitarian gesture.' Unfortunately, the request was rejected," Franziska Brantner, co-chair of the Greens, told DW on Thursday in Warsaw. Green co-leader Franziska Brantner hasn't given up hope that Germany will still change its stance on Polish reparations Image: Michaela Küfner/DW "Hope dies last, so we will do everything in our power to ensure that the coalition makes this change after all," she emphasized. Brantner sees the budget committee's "final review session," which will take place this week, as a last chance. The issue of reparations still plays an important role in Polish society, even more than 80 years after the end of the war. There is hardly a family that did not suffer during the war. In the latest German-Polish Barometer — a representative survey that has been conducted for 25 years — 53% of respondents stated that the suffering of the Polish people is not sufficiently acknowledged in Germany. Only 18% believed that the Germans have done enough. Poland wants WWII reparations To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video German private donors support the victims' fund Jakub Deka, chairman of the Foundation for Polish–German Reconciliation, believes the appeal by the victims' associations could now mobilize Germany's civil society. Following an initial appeal in May directed at the German federal government, several hundred Germans responded with donations ranging from €50 to several hundred euros. To date, a total of more than €35,000 ($39,000) has been deposited into the foundation's account. Several people in need have already received one-time assistance from this fund. "It's a drop in the bucket, but every little bit helps," Deka told DW. The foundation's chairman quotes Jerzy Tarasiewicz — who led the victims' association in the Polish city of Gdansk for many years — as a cautionary reminder. In January, Tarasiewicz was quoted in an interview with the daily newspaper Gazeta Wyborcza as saying: "They [the Germans] are waiting for us to die." Tarasiewicz, who was born in 1942 on a German farm where his parents were performing forced labor, died in late September at the age of 84 without being able to witness this "humanitarian gesture." "It is a painful reminder that the victims cannot wait any longer," said Deka. This article was originally written in German.
